newsitem.title: USA: Apparel dresses-up October sales, but electronics lag.
newsitem.headline: Apparel dresses-up October sales, but electronics lag.

text.p: Apparel helped lift retailers to moderate sales gains in October, but electronics continued to lag with no blockbuster product in sight to help the sector in the upcoming holiday season.

Overall, December is seen shaping up favourably for retailers. Confident consumers, leaner inventories and easier comparisons with the previous year are expected to offset a shorter selling period between Thanskgiving and Christmas and concerns about consumer debt levels.
"I think in spite of everything, we will have a decent Christmas," said Karen Sack, retail analyst at Standard and Poor's.

Sales in October were in line with expectations, analysts said. The Salomon Brothers same-store sales index showed 4.8 percent growth, up from 0.4 percent a year ago and 3.7 percent in September. Same-stores sales refer to sales at stores that were open a year ago, and do not include new locations.
"October sales were positively impacted by an improving environment for apparel, more seasonal weather and relatively easy comparisons," Salomon Brothers' analysts said in a research report.
Sears, Roebuck and Co. cited apparel for helping it post a 5.3 percent increase in comparable domestic store sales for October.

"Women's ready to wear had strong growth, led by outerwear and sportswear such as leather jackets, sweaters and jeans," Sears Chief Executive Arthur Martinez said in a statement. "Sales of children's and men's apparel showed double-digit increases, as did cosmetics and fine jewelry."

Gap Inc., the casual clothing retailer, reported same-store sales up 4.8 percent, compared with a 0.4 percent gain a year ago. J.C. Penney Co. said its same-store sales rose 13.1 percent, but analysts noted that a change in the company's reporting period helped boost its comparison.

Overall, department store same-store sales were up 5.9 percent, discount stores rose 4.8 percent, apparel was up 5.1 percent and hard goods were down 5.7 percent, according to Dean Witter Reynolds' index.
Dean Witter analyst Patrick McCormack said sales as a whole were up 4 percent on a same-store basis.

A shift in when Halloween fell in the four-week reporting period may have helped boost discount store sales, he said. Halloween was in the end of the October reporting period this year, whereas the holiday fell in the beginning of the November 1995 period.

Meanwhile, tough competition and declining consumer purchases pressured sales at electronics stores. Best Buy Co. Inc. was especially hard hit, posting a 15 percent decline in comparable store sales and forecasting a negative comparison in November with healthy year-ago gains.
Despite an increase in customers, average transactions fell 13 percent due to industry-wide weakness in personal computer sales, Best Buy chief financial officer Allen Lenzmeier said.

"In addition, consumer electronics remained very soft and broadly competitive," he said. "The sales decline was also attributable to difficult comparisons to last October, which benefited from highly effective extended consumer financing promotions."

Analysts were also hard-pressed to come up with a major new item for the Christmas season that might boost sales in the consumer electronics sector. "For that end of it, it's probably a bad Christmas season," said Michael Niemira, economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd.

Overall, Dean Witter's McCormack said he expects December same-store sales to gain 2 to 3 percent. He noted that retailers are keeping inventories leaner, which could lead to less discounting and promotions in December.

Standard and Poor's Sack also noted the trend in better inventory management by retailers, saying December sales could be up 5 percent. Bargains could be harder to find than last year, when Christmas sales were generally regarded as disappointing.
"It will be harder than last year," Sack said. "(But) there'll still be sales and promotions. That's part of every holiday."
